facts.detail: Web Serial lets a web page talk to a USB serial device after the reader picks it in the browser's own dialog. Chrome, Edge and Opera support it on computers; Firefox added it in version 151. Safari does not support it.
facts.label: Browsers that can talk to USB boards
facts.value: Firefox 151 (19 May 2026) joined Chrome and Edge in supporting Web Serial

facts.detail: YoWASP packages Yosys and nextpnr as WebAssembly; its author describes synthesis, placement, routing and programming running entirely in the browser, including on a phone.
facts.label: FPGA tools in the browser
facts.value: A complete open FPGA flow (Yosys, nextpnr) runs inside a web browser

facts.detail: Espressif's ESP32-C3 is a Wi-Fi and Bluetooth microcontroller built on a RISC-V core; boards with it cost a few dollars and run MicroPython.
facts.label: ESP32-C3
facts.value: Single-core 32-bit RISC-V at 160 MHz

facts.detail: WCH's CH32V003 has 2 KB of SRAM and 16 KB of flash; a development board was offered for $6.90 at launch in 2022.
facts.label: A RISC-V chip for under 10 cents
facts.unchecked: Not re-checked on 2026-11-25: the source's site blocks automated reads (a bot challenge). It needs a person with a browser, or a newer source (#378).
facts.value: WCH CH32V003: a 32-bit RISC-V microcontroller for less than 10 cents

facts.detail: About a fifth of the roughly 100 W a resting adult uses; textbook estimates collected by The Physics Factbook.
facts.label: Power used by a human brain
facts.value: About 20 W

facts.detail: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light, close to X-rays; the deep-ultraviolet light used before it has a wavelength of 193 nm.
facts.label: Wavelength of the light in the newest chip-printing machines

facts.detail: “On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem”, submitted in 1936: no general method can decide every such yes-or-no question.
facts.label: Questions no machine can settle
facts.value: Proved by Alan Turing in 1936

facts.detail: TSMC's figures for its N2 process against N3E, compiled by Tom's Hardware. The density is for a 'mixed' chip of 50% logic, 30% SRAM and 20% analog; logic alone gains more, memory less. Used for the chip model's rules for a newer generation (src/engines/chip.js).
facts.label: What one new generation gives (TSMC N2 against N3E)
facts.value: About 1.15× the transistors in the same area, 10–15% faster at the same power, or 25–30% less power at the same speed

facts.detail: Ioffe Institute, New Semiconductor Materials archive, silicon at 300 K: band gap 1.12 eV; electron mobility up to 1,400 and hole mobility up to 450 cm²/V·s; melts at 1,412 °C.
facts.label: Silicon: gap, mobilities, melting point
facts.value: Gap 1.12 eV; electrons 1,400, holes 450 cm²/V·s; melts at 1,412 °C

facts.detail: Ioffe Institute, New Semiconductor Materials archive, germanium at 300 K: band gap 0.66 eV; electron mobility up to 3,900 and hole mobility up to 1,900 cm²/V·s; melts at 937 °C.
facts.label: Germanium: gap, mobilities, melting point
facts.value: Gap 0.66 eV; electrons 3,900, holes 1,900 cm²/V·s; melts at 937 °C

facts.detail: Ioffe Institute, New Semiconductor Materials archive, Ga0.47In0.53As (the alloy matched to indium phosphide) at 300 K: band gap 0.74 eV; electron Hall mobility about 12,000 cm²/V·s in weakly doped material; hole mobility at most 300 cm²/V·s; melts at about 1,100 °C.
facts.label: Indium gallium arsenide: gap, mobilities, melting point
facts.value: Gap 0.74 eV; electrons about 12,000, holes at most 300 cm²/V·s; melts at about 1,100 °C

facts.detail: Gallium nitride (wurtzite): band gap 3.39 eV at 300 K and melting point 2,500 °C (Ioffe Institute NSM archive); electrons in the thin sheet under an AlGaN layer, the channel of a GaN transistor, reach over 2,000 cm²/V·s at room temperature (Jena et al., UC Santa Barbara, 2001, citing Gaska et al. 1998); holes measured at about 31 cm²/V·s (Poncé, Jena and Giustino, 2019).
facts.label: Gallium nitride: gap, mobilities, melting point
facts.source: Ioffe Institute; Jena et al.; Poncé et al.
facts.value: Gap 3.39 eV; electrons about 2,000 (in its transistors), holes about 31 cm²/V·s; melts at 2,500 °C

facts.detail: One layer of molybdenum disulfide has a direct band gap of 1.8 eV (Mak, Lee, Hone, Shan and Heinz, Physical Review Letters 105, 136805, 2010). Grown below 300 °C on a 200 mm wafer, so it can go on top of a finished chip, its electrons reached about 36 cm²/V·s (Zhu et al., Nature Nanotechnology, 2023). Switches that use holes in it are hard to make: controllable p-type doping of these materials has proved challenging (Wang et al., Nature 610, 2022).
facts.label: Molybdenum disulfide (one layer): gap and mobility
facts.source: Physical Review Letters; Nature Nanotechnology; Nature
facts.value: Gap 1.8 eV; electrons about 36 cm²/V·s when grown cool enough for a chip; holes not yet usable

facts.detail: Zhu et al., Low-thermal-budget synthesis of monolayer molybdenum disulfide for silicon back-end-of-line integration on a 200 mm platform (Nature Nanotechnology, 2023): once a chip's transistors are made, the steps that build its wiring above them must stay below 400 °C.
facts.label: How hot the steps above a chip's transistors may get
facts.value: Below 400 °C once the transistors are made

facts.detail: Dürkop, Getty, Cobas and Fuhrer, Extraordinary Mobility in Semiconducting Carbon Nanotubes (Nano Letters 4, 35, 2004): an intrinsic mobility above 100,000 cm²/V·s at room temperature. A tube's band gap is about 0.8 eV divided by its diameter in nanometres, so about 0.6 to 0.8 eV for the tubes used in transistors; electrons and holes have mirror-image bands.
facts.label: Carbon nanotubes: gap and mobility
facts.value: Mobility above 100,000 cm²/V·s; gap about 0.7 eV

facts.detail: Hills et al., Modern microprocessor built from complementary carbon nanotube transistors (Nature 572, 595, 2019): RV16X-NANO, a 16-bit RISC-V processor of more than 14,000 carbon-nanotube transistors, both kinds, made with steps that a silicon factory uses and at temperatures low enough to build above other circuits.
facts.label: A processor made of carbon-nanotube transistors
facts.value: RV16X-NANO: 14,000+ nanotube transistors, both kinds (2019)

facts.detail: Schwierz, Graphene transistors (Nature Nanotechnology 5, 487, 2010): graphene has no band gap, so a switch of large-area graphene cannot be turned off; the on-off ratios reported are about 2 to 20, where logic needs 10,000 to 10 million. Its review plots mobility against band gap for many materials: the wider the gap, the slower the carriers. Graphene's mobility on a substrate is about 10,000 cm²/V·s (Novoselov et al., Science, 2004).
facts.label: Graphene: no gap, so it never turns off
facts.value: On-off ratio about 2–20; logic needs 10,000 or more

facts.detail: Ionescu and Riel, Tunnel field-effect transistors as energy-efficient electronic switches (Nature 479, 329, 2011): a switch whose carriers go over a barrier needs at least (kT/q) ln 10, about 60 mV at room temperature, of gate voltage for each tenfold more current, which is why the supply voltage stopped falling; carriers that tunnel through the barrier instead are not bound by it.
facts.label: The 60 mV per tenfold limit on a switch
facts.value: At least about 60 mV per tenfold at room temperature

facts.detail: Sarkar et al., A subthermionic tunnel field-effect transistor with an atomically thin channel (Nature 526, 91, 2015): electrons tunnelling from germanium into two layers of molybdenum disulfide turned on at an average of 31.1 mV per tenfold over four tenfolds of current, at room temperature.
facts.label: A tunnelling switch steeper than 60 mV
facts.value: 31.1 mV per tenfold over four tenfolds (2015)

facts.detail: Salahuddin and Datta proposed a ferroelectric layer in the gate that acts as a negative capacitance and amplifies the gate's voltage (Nano Letters 8, 405, 2008). Si et al., Steep-slope hysteresis-free negative capacitance MoS2 transistors (Nature Nanotechnology 13, 24, 2018), measured a turn-on steeper than 60 mV per tenfold, essentially without hysteresis; whether the effect lasts at a chip's speeds is still argued.
facts.label: Negative capacitance: a switch steeper than 60 mV
facts.value: Steeper than 60 mV per tenfold, shown in a lab (2018)

facts.detail: CSET's estimate of the foundry sale price of a 300 mm wafer in 2020 (Khan and Mann, AI Chips: What They Are and Why They Matter, Table 9). Used for the chip model's wafer cost per generation (src/engines/chip.js).
facts.label: Price of one wafer, by process (2020)

facts.detail: Elsner et al., Measuring the environmental impact of delivering AI at Google scale (August 2025): the median Gemini Apps text prompt in May 2025, counting the accelerators, the host machines, idle machines kept ready and the data centre's overhead. The accelerators alone came to about 0.10 Wh. Google's own measurement of its own service.
facts.label: Energy of one AI answer (measured)
facts.value: The median text prompt used 0.24 Wh, of which the AI chips themselves used about 0.10 Wh (May 2025)

facts.detail: Epoch AI (February 2025): one second of an H100 at 1,500 W and 70% of its power for a typical GPT-4o query; a pessimistic estimate, and far higher for long inputs (about 2.5 Wh for 10,000 tokens in) and for reasoning models.
facts.label: Energy of one ChatGPT query (estimated)
facts.value: About 0.3 Wh for a typical query

facts.detail: Boroumand et al., Google Workloads for Consumer Devices: Mitigating Data Movement Bottlenecks (ASPLOS 2018): Chrome, TensorFlow Mobile and video on phones and tablets; doing simple functions inside the memory cut total energy by 55% on average.
facts.label: Energy spent moving data in a phone
facts.value: About 63% of the whole device's energy goes to moving data between memory and the processors

facts.detail: Schroeder, Pinheiro and Weber, DRAM Errors in the Wild: A Large-Scale Field Study (SIGMETRICS 2009): Google's server fleet over two and a half years (32.2% of machines, 8.2% of memory modules). The paper gives 25,000 to 70,000 errors per billion device-hours per megabit, and many errors come back in the same place: hard faults, not one-off flips.
facts.label: Memory errors in a server fleet
facts.value: About a third of machines and over 8% of memory modules saw at least one correctable error a year; 1.3% of machines saw an uncorrectable one

facts.detail: The Llama 3 Herd of Models (Meta, 2024), section 3.3.4 and table 5: 466 interruptions in a 54-day snapshot of pre-training, 47 of them planned. GPU issues were the largest category (58.7%).
facts.label: Interruptions while training a large AI model
facts.value: 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days on 16,384 GPUs, about 78% from hardware; 6 from silent data corruption

facts.detail: Hochschild et al., Cores that don't count (HotOS 2021): cores that compute wrong answers silently and only sometimes, "similar to the rate reported by Facebook".
facts.label: Cores that quietly compute wrong answers (Google)
facts.value: A few mercurial cores per several thousand machines

facts.detail: At sea level the reference flux of neutrons above 10 MeV is about 13 per cm² per hour (New York City, JEDEC's reference spectrum, as given in S. E. Rauch's IEEE lecture on terrestrial soft errors).
facts.label: Neutrons from cosmic rays at altitude
facts.value: About 300 times more neutrons at cruising altitude than at sea level

facts.detail: S. E. Rauch, Terrestrial Radiation Induced Soft Errors in Integrated Circuits (IEEE Electron Devices Society lecture), on a 1994 IBM memory study: "the relative alpha and cosmic contributions are about equal at sea level". The share depends on the package.
facts.label: Where bit flips come from at sea level
facts.value: Alpha particles from the chip's own materials and neutrons from cosmic rays cause about as many flips each

facts.detail: Ultra-low-alpha grade from Solstice (formerly Honeywell); IBM gives the same specification (under 2 alpha particles per 1,000 hours per cm²). Ordinary solder bumps emit 20 to 100 per 1,000 hours per cm² (Rauch's lecture).
facts.label: Low-alpha materials for packages
facts.value: Ultra-low-alpha materials emit under 0.002 alpha particles per cm² per hour, ten or more times less than ordinary solder

facts.detail: Tezzaron's white paper (2004) gives 1,000 to 5,000 FIT per megabit for memory of its time; Rauch's lecture projects about 300 FIT per megabit from cosmic rays alone for SRAM, with the rate per bit nearly flat as chips shrink. Measurements differ by orders of magnitude between parts.
facts.label: How often radiation flips a bit of on-chip memory
facts.value: Hundreds to a few thousand flips per billion hours for each megabit at sea level

facts.detail: Bentoutou, Performance Comparison of Real Time EDAC Systems for Applications On-Board Small Satellites (2011): the Alsat-1 satellite, 686 km sun-synchronous orbit, Samsung SRAM, 265,649 errors logged in 2,622 days (2002 to 2010). About ten thousand times a sea-level rate of 1,000 FIT per megabit.
facts.label: Bit flips in a satellite's memory
facts.source: Int. J. of Electrical and Computer Engineering (Bentoutou)
facts.value: About 4 × 10⁻⁷ flips per bit per day in low Earth orbit

facts.detail: Xilinx (AMD) XAPP645, Single Error Correction and Double Error Detection (2006): the (72,64) Hamming code. Seven check bits are the fewest that correct one error in 64 bits; the eighth detects two.
facts.label: Error-correcting memory: the extra bits
facts.value: 8 check bits for every 64 data bits (12.5% more) correct any one flipped bit and detect any two

facts.detail: ISO 26262-5:2018 hardware metrics at the highest safety level (ASIL D), as tabled by Battery Design: a probabilistic metric for random hardware failures under 10 FIT, a single-point fault metric of at least 99% and a latent fault metric of at least 90%.
facts.label: What a car's brakes ask of a chip (ASIL D)
facts.value: Under 10 failures in a billion hours, with at least 99% of single faults caught

facts.detail: Li et al., Understanding Error Propagation in Deep Learning Neural Network (DNN) Accelerators and Applications (SC17, NVIDIA): single bit flips in the accelerator's datapath latches; 0.38% with floating point, up to 7.19% with a 32-bit fixed-point format. Only high-order bits matter, and about 84% of faults are masked by pooling or ReLU.
facts.label: How often one flipped bit changes an AI's answer
facts.value: 0.4% to 7% of single bit flips changed AlexNet's top answer, depending on the number format

facts.detail: As stated by AIST, which developed it; Yokogawa offers device prototyping on Minimal Fab lines.
facts.label: Minimal Fab (AIST)
facts.value: No cleanroom; half-inch (12.5 mm) wafers; manufacturing cost cut to 1/100 to 1/1000

facts.detail: From Pragmatic's own manufacturing page; FlexLogic lines run in Sedgefield, with a second line being built in Durham.
facts.label: Pragmatic FlexLogic cycle time
facts.value: Production cycle time under 48 hours, against several months for a typical silicon fab

facts.detail: Pragmatic's claim, reported when it raised money for a second fab in Durham (December 2022).
facts.label: Cost of a FlexLogic line
facts.value: A FlexLogic facility can be built for a hundredth of the cost of a standard fab

facts.detail: The Z2, finished in August 2021 with salvaged and homemade equipment in his family's garage; the same 10 µm polysilicon-gate process as Intel's first microprocessor.
facts.label: Chips made in a garage (Sam Zeloof)
facts.value: 1,200 transistors on one homemade chip, at 10 µm

facts.detail: Founded in 2022 by Jim Keller and Sam Zeloof as Atomic Semi; renamed Fab2 and moved to Texas in July 2026.
facts.label: Fab2 (formerly Atomic Semi)
facts.value: A "fab fab": a factory that mass-produces small chip fabs and the tools inside them

facts.detail: Pragmatic's comparison, written to recruit fab engineers: under a week for its flexible line.
facts.label: Tape-out to tested wafer
facts.value: 18 to 26 weeks from tape-out to wafer test data for silicon; under a week on FlexLogic

facts.detail: Bloom, Jones, Van Reenen and Webb, American Economic Review 110(4), 2020. Research productivity on chips fell about 6.8% a year.
facts.label: Are ideas getting harder to find?
facts.value: Keeping chip density doubling takes more than 18 times as many researchers as in the early 1970s

facts.detail: Nagy, Farmer, Bui and Trancik, PLOS ONE 8(2), 2013: six proposed laws tested by hindcasting on the cost and production of 62 technologies.
facts.label: Wright's law against Moore's law
facts.value: Cost falling as a power of how much has been made (Wright, 1936) forecast best; Moore's law came close

facts.detail: Kuon and Rose, IEEE Transactions on CAD 26(2), 2007, at 90 nm, for logic-only circuits; hard memories and multipliers narrow the area and power gaps.
facts.label: The gap between an FPGA and a custom chip
facts.value: About 14× the dynamic power, 3.4 to 4.6× slower, about 35× the area

facts.detail: Measured on one board: the whole chip through JTAG, part of it through JTAG, and the same part through the chip's internal port with DMA.
facts.label: How long an FPGA takes to rewire
facts.value: Whole chip 3.8 s; part of it 209 ms, or 324 µs through the internal port

facts.detail: A 40 nm test chip from the National University of Singapore, rewired word by word on every clock cycle.
facts.label: A coarse-grained array (HyCUBE)
facts.value: 28.6× the power efficiency of an FPGA platform, 26.5× an ARM core

facts.detail: DARPA's program for radios whose signals change faster than an FPGA can be rewired.
facts.label: DARPA PROWESS
facts.value: Processors that reconfigure themselves within 50 nanoseconds (a goal)

facts.detail: Adrian Thompson, University of Sussex, 1996: evolution configured 100 cells of an FPGA to tell two tones apart; the circuit used the chip's own physics.
facts.label: A circuit evolved on an FPGA
facts.value: It worked, and depended on cells with no connection to the output

facts.detail: A mature 180–130 nm hybrid process first developed by Cypress Semiconductor; the open kit was first released as an experimental preview, and is now kept by the CHIPS Alliance.
facts.label: SKY130, the first open process design kit
facts.value: Released in May 2020 by Google and SkyWater: a 130 nm process with 1 layer of local interconnect and 5 of metal

facts.detail: Includes digital standard cell libraries, low-, medium- and high-voltage devices, SRAM blocks and I/O cells. Tiny Tapeout and wafer.space now run shuttles on it.
facts.label: GF180MCU, the second open process design kit
facts.value: Released in August 2022 by Google and GlobalFoundries under the Apache 2.0 licence: a 180 nm process with up to 5 layers of metal

facts.detail: From the summary of key periphery rules; the full rule set covers every layer and every kind of part.
facts.label: Two of SKY130’s design rules
facts.value: Metal 1 at least 0.14 µm wide and 0.14 µm from its neighbour; a via at least 0.15 µm across and 0.17 µm from the next

facts.detail: The PDK’s mask table lists 51 masks the line can print and marks 34 as used on SKY130: wells, gates and implants for the transistors, contacts, local interconnect, five metals and their vias, and layers for the pads and packaging. A plain logic tile draws only a few of them itself.
facts.label: Masks on SKY130
facts.value: 34 masks marked as used on SKY130

facts.detail: From the 2024 Wilson Research Group functional verification study for Siemens EDA, as reported by Semiconductor Engineering; logic and function errors remain the most common reason for a respin (making the masks again).
facts.label: Chips that work the first time they are made
facts.value: 14% of projects worked on first silicon in 2024, down from about 30% historically

facts.detail: Verilog was created at Gateway Design Automation in the 1980s with its simulator, Verilog-XL; SystemVerilog adds checking features and is the language most chips are now described and tested in.
facts.label: Verilog as a standard
facts.value: IEEE 1364 since 1995; SystemVerilog, IEEE 1800, since 2005

facts.detail: Set by the I/O pads of the SKY130 chip, whose documentation gives a maximum input frequency of 66 MHz; the demo board’s clock can be set from 1 Hz to 66.5 MHz.
facts.label: The fastest clock on a Tiny Tapeout chip
facts.value: Around 66 MHz

facts.detail: One shared chip on SkyWater’s 130 nm process, each design on its own tile, picked by a selector on the chip.
facts.label: Designs on one Tiny Tapeout chip
facts.value: 273 designs on the SKY 26b chip

facts.detail: Efabless ran the free shuttles Google paid for on SKY130 and GF180. Its founders then started ChipFoundry to restore access to SkyWater’s 130 nm process; Tiny Tapeout moved to IHP, SkyWater and GlobalFoundries runs through new partners.
facts.label: When the shared-run company closed
facts.value: Efabless closed in March 2025, delaying about 500 Tiny Tapeout designs

facts.detail: Light travels 299,792,458 metres a second, exactly (the SI definition); one tick of a 3 GHz clock lasts a third of a nanosecond, in which light covers 9.99 cm. A signal in a copper wire on a board travels at about half that speed.
facts.label: How far light goes in one tick of a 3 GHz clock
facts.value: About 10 cm

facts.detail: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (Bell System Technical Journal, 1948): a channel of bandwidth B and signal-to-noise ratio S/N carries at most B log2(1 + S/N) bits a second without error; more noise or more distance means fewer bits through the same wire.
facts.label: Shannon's limit on a noisy channel
facts.value: At most B log2(1 + S/N) bits a second (1948)

facts.detail: Landauer, Information is Physical (Physics Today, 1991): information is always carried by something physical (a charge, a spin, a hole in a card), so its handling obeys physics; erasing a bit costs at least kT ln 2 of heat.
facts.label: Information is physical
facts.value: Every bit rides on something physical (1991)

facts.detail: Wulf and McKee, Hitting the Memory Wall: Implications of the Obvious (Computer Architecture News, 1995), citing microprocessor performance growing about 80% a year and DRAM speed about 7% a year: if the gap kept growing, a processor would soon spend most of its time waiting for memory.
facts.label: The memory wall
facts.value: Processors about 80% faster a year, memory about 7% (1995)

facts.detail: O'Connor et al., Fine-Grained DRAM: Energy-Efficient DRAM for Extreme Bandwidth Systems (MICRO 2017, NVIDIA Research): accessing a bit in an HBM2 stack costs about 3.97 pJ, most of it moving the bit inside the DRAM and across to the processor.
facts.label: Energy to read one bit from stacked memory (HBM2)
facts.value: About 4 pJ a bit

facts.detail: The Register, 22 November 2025: a pluggable optical transceiver draws 9 to 15 W depending on its speed (about 11 to 19 pJ a bit at 800 Gb/s); Nvidia says its co-packaged optics switches are up to 3.5 times more energy efficient, and Broadcom that they could cut optics power by 65%. Light's energy per bit hardly grows with distance.
facts.label: Power of optical links between chips
facts.value: Pluggable optics 9–15 W each; co-packaged up to 3.5× more efficient

facts.detail: BioNumbers 108982, from Zalc, Goujet and Colman (Current Biology, 2008): an action potential travels 50 to 100 m/s along a myelinated axon of a vertebrate; a bare fibre is far slower.
facts.label: Speed of a signal along a myelinated nerve
facts.value: 50 to 100 m/s

facts.detail: The Llama 3 Herd of Models (Meta, 2024), Table 4: training the 405-billion-parameter model used 38% to 43% of the GPUs' peak arithmetic (BF16 model FLOPs utilization) on 8,192 to 16,384 H100s; the rest of the time went to waiting for data, communication and other overheads.
facts.label: How much of an AI cluster's arithmetic is used
facts.value: 38–43% of peak while training Llama 3 405B

facts.detail: In April 1965 Gordon Moore projected that the components on one chip would double every year, from about 64 to as many as 65,000 by 1975. In 1975 he revised the rate to a doubling every two years.
facts.label: Moore's first rule, and his second
facts.value: Doubling every year (1965), then every two years (1975)

facts.label: The generations of chipmaking, by year
facts.value: From 10 µm (1971) to 2 nm (2025)

facts.detail: Intel's node names matched the transistor's gate length from 10 µm (1972) to 0.35 µm (1995); since about 1997 a node's name is not the size of anything on the chip. The "3 nm" generation has a gate pitch of about 48 nm and a metal pitch of about 24 nm.
facts.label: What a node's name measures
facts.value: "3 nm": gate pitch about 48 nm, metal pitch about 24 nm

facts.detail: By 2004 Intel’s fastest desktop chips reached a clock barrier at 3.8 GHz, set by heat and power (130 W); the industry turned to slower chips with two cores on one die.
facts.label: When the clock stopped climbing
facts.value: About 3.8 GHz, 2004

facts.detail: Intel's Pentium D and AMD's Athlon 64 X2, the first dual-core desktop processors, both came out in May 2005, because faster clocks were only adding heat.
facts.label: The first dual-core desktop chips
facts.value: May 2005

facts.detail: AlexNet, which won the ImageNet challenge in 2012, was trained for five to six days on two NVIDIA GTX 580 graphics chips.
facts.label: Deep learning on graphics chips
facts.source: Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton (Communications of the ACM)
facts.value: Two GTX 580 GPUs, 2012

facts.detail: AMD's EPYC Rome (2019) puts eight 7 nm compute chiplets of eight cores each around one 14 nm input/output die: nine pieces of silicon, 64 cores, in one package.
facts.label: A processor made of chiplets
facts.value: Nine dies, 64 cores (2019)

facts.detail: The lattice parameter of an ideal crystal of pure, naturally occurring silicon in vacuum at 22.5 °C: 5.431 020 511 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. The crystal's cube of atoms repeats at this spacing.
facts.label: Silicon's crystal repeats
facts.value: The silicon crystal repeats every 0.543 nm (5.431 × 10⁻¹⁰ m)

facts.detail: Nielsen et al., Genetic circuit design automation, Science 352 (2016), aac7341. Cello turns a circuit written in Verilog into a DNA sequence for E. coli, with gates made of repressors (NOT and NOR). Of 60 circuits designed, 45 worked correctly in every output state, and 92% of 412 output states worked as predicted; building them took 880,000 base pairs of DNA.
facts.label: Verilog compiled into DNA for living cells (Cello)
facts.value: 60 circuits designed, 45 correct in every output state, 92% of 412 output states as predicted

facts.detail: Qian and Winfree, Scaling up digital circuit computation with DNA strand displacement cascades, Science 332 (2011), 1196. Every gate has a threshold and catalysis (fuel) to restore the signal; the largest circuit computes the square root of a four-bit number.
facts.label: Logic circuits of DNA strands in a test tube (seesaw gates)
facts.value: a four-bit square-root circuit of 130 DNA strands

facts.detail: Cherry and Qian, Scaling up molecular pattern recognition with DNA-based winner-take-all neural networks, Nature 559 (2018), 370. Each pattern is 20 DNA molecules chosen from 100 that stand for the bits of a 10 x 10 picture of a handwritten digit; test patterns had up to 30 of the 100 bits flipped.
facts.label: A DNA neural network that sorts patterns into nine kinds
facts.value: up to nine categories, 10 x 10 patterns, up to 30 of 100 bits flipped

facts.detail: Each domino falls once: the chain is a circuit that must be stood up again by hand before the next sum.
facts.label: A computer made of 10,000 dominoes
facts.value: Matt Parker’s chain of 10,000 dominoes adds any two 4-bit binary numbers (2014)

facts.detail: An analog computer built by a student at the London School of Economics; valves stand for taxes and the supply of money.
facts.label: A computer that runs on water
facts.value: Bill Phillips’s MONIAC, 1949: water flowing through tanks and pipes models a country’s economy

facts.detail: The first computation done with molecules: every possible route was made at once as strands, and the right one fished out.
facts.label: A route found by DNA in a test tube
facts.value: Leonard Adleman’s seven-city route problem, solved with strands of DNA in 1994

facts.detail: Lulu Qian and Erik Winfree’s circuit of strand-displacement gates, the largest biochemical circuit of its time.
facts.label: A logic circuit made of DNA
facts.value: 74 DNA molecules work out the square root of any number up to 15, in about 10 hours (2011)

facts.detail: Kevin Cherry and Lulu Qian’s winner-take-all network: each digit is a 10 by 10 pattern, one kind of molecule per pixel.
facts.label: A neural network made of DNA
facts.value: A test tube of DNA strands recognises handwritten digits from 1 to 9, written as mixes of molecules (2018)

facts.detail: A cell turns a gene on only when it needs what the gene makes: chemistry that decides.
facts.label: How a cell switches its genes
facts.value: Nobel Prize 1965 to François Jacob, André Lwoff and Jacques Monod, for how cells control their genes

facts.detail: Timothy Gardner, Charles Cantor and James Collins; it stays in the state it was flipped to, so it also keeps one bit.
facts.label: A switch built into bacteria
facts.value: A two-state genetic toggle switch in E. coli, flipped by a brief dose of a chemical (2000)

facts.detail: Two designs: a cascade of RNA and a cascade of memory units that flip a piece of DNA.
facts.label: Bacteria that count
facts.value: Synthetic genetic counters in E. coli count up to three events (Science, 2009)

facts.detail: The same language that describes chips, compiled into DNA instead of masks.
facts.label: Circuits written in Verilog, grown in bacteria
facts.value: Cello: 60 circuits written in a chip designer’s language, 45 worked in E. coli on the first test; the largest had seven logic gates (2016)

changes.title: The lattice: matter that computes
changes.summary: Nine facts for the Map's second arrangement, matter and layers: computers of dominoes and water, DNA that finds a route, takes a square root and recognises digits, and cells that switch, count and run circuits written in Verilog.

changes.title: Is it true? The block and Machines audited
changes.summary: Every factual sentence at the block level and in Machines from shared blocks was checked against a source and given a verdict (docs/reviews/truth/block-and-machines.md). Two new figures: the share of power a chip's clock takes, and the reversible test chip against a regular one; the custom chip against a general processor rechecked.

changes.title: The bench meets Why perfect designs fail
changes.summary: Three real-world failures, hands-on: give the factory test a small budget and watch a defect escape, sort a wafer with a design bug from one with a broken chip, and pull a wire loose to see a chip change its mind. The reliability topic now points to each experiment.

changes.title: A gentler first visit
changes.summary: The tour no longer opens by itself. The map now offers three ways to start (build a chip, break a perfect design, imagine a what-if), and small tips appear only when a feature becomes useful, never again once you have used it. Tips can be turned off; the 30-second tour is still there for anyone who wants it.

changes.title: One bench program for many boards
changes.summary: An open MicroPython program turns an ESP32, a Raspberry Pi Pico or another MicroPython board into a pin driver for the bench, and the page can install it with no tools. Test a real 74HC00 (four NAND gates) on a breadboard against its simulation, with the wiring shown for each board. Any board can now be checked against the Open Bench Protocol. Two new facts on cheap RISC-V chips.

changes.title: Your bench: real hardware, step 0
changes.summary: A new build topic: put a design on a board, try it by hand, and twin-test it against the simulation, then find the faulty chip in a tray by the pattern of its wrong answers. The bench talks to boards through the Open Bench Protocol, a few text commands any board can answer. The virtual board works today; the Tiny Tapeout demo board and any Open Bench board can be tried as experiments. Four new facts on Web Serial, the demo board, the Pico 2 and FPGA tools in the browser.

changes.title: New topic: why perfect designs fail
changes.summary: A Big questions layer opens with a reliability stress test for phones, cars, data centers and satellites, and seven real cases from the Pentium division bug to unstable 2024 desktop chips. Eight new facts.

changes.title: What if? The map as a simulator
changes.summary: Move a lever on the map, such as AI demand, HBM supply, the price of electricity, a late process node or a shortage of ordinary chips, and watch the effect ripple across the connected topics, with the cause chain behind every change. Four puzzles, four ready-made scenarios and four new facts on the 2021 car-chip shortage, Intel's 10 nm delay, the 2026 memory squeeze and what an AI data center costs.

changes.title: My chip
changes.summary: One chip that is yours, carried through every layer: design it in the tiny chip studio and every topic page shows what that layer means for it. A passport collects a stamp for each stage, with a downloadable chip card.

changes.title: New ways to compute
changes.summary: A new layer on the map with eight topics: beyond von Neumann, compute in memory, neuromorphic, photonic, quantum, probabilistic, reversible, and dataflow and wafer-scale. Each has a simulation. Sixteen new facts on the state of each field in 2026.

changes.title: Design with an AI agent
changes.summary: New topic: an agent proposes designs, code, estimates and facts, and you check them with the lab's engines before deciding what to trust. Inside Claude, a live agent designs tiny chips for you to verify.

changes.title: Time machine: 1971 to 2040
changes.summary: Drag through the years and the site follows: the map, every topic page, the company explorer and the roadmap. History to 2026, labelled plans and projections after. Three new facts on design costs and the transistor trend.

changes.title: From simulation to real silicon
changes.summary: Every tiny-chip design now exports as a ready Tiny Tapeout project: Verilog, info.yaml, a cocotb test and the gate netlist. CI checks every export with Icarus Verilog and Yosys. Four facts on shuttles, costs and the open flow.

changes.title: Build the CPU from your own gates
changes.summary: New tiny-chip project: one bit of an ALU. The RISC-V lab chains 32 copies and runs every add, compare and branch on your gates. A bug in your slice, or a planted factory defect, breaks the CPU.

changes.title: Every chip, not only AI chips
changes.summary: The lab now covers every kind of chip. New topic Chips everywhere: look inside a phone, car, thermostat, laptop and AI server, and match jobs to the right kind of chip. Seven new facts on chip sales, units, end markets and car chips.

changes.title: One project: Open Silicon Lab
changes.summary: Silicon Journey Lab and Open Silicon Quest merged into one open-source project with a connected chip-stack map. Facts now live in this file and are updated by pull request.
Added Google TPU Ironwood, AWS Trainium3, Microsoft Maia 200, Cerebras CS-4, NVIDIA Groq 3 LPU, TPU 8t/8i and Trainium4, and updated AMD MI455X to 23.3 TB/s and 320 billion transistors.
changes.title: Eight AI-chip facts added

changes.summary: 33 key facts across six chapters verified against their sources. From now on they are rechecked at the start of every month, and each change is logged here.
changes.title: Fact base launched

changes.summary: Added a sand-to-switch physics stage with a crystal puller and implant lab, a memory, network and data-center stage, and a scenario planner with a beyond-silicon maturity board. 5 new tracked facts.
